planting.note: Scatter seed in fall among established sagebrush-steppe grasses such as bluebunch wheatgrass; this species is hemiparasitic on nearby roots and rarely persists if sown alone in bare soil.

directions: Wyoming's state flower is a tall, slender paintbrush of dry sagebrush steppe and open pine woodland across the Great Basin and Rocky Mountain foothills, sending up narrow, gray-green leaves and elongated spikes of scarlet-to-orange bracts from late spring into midsummer. Like other paintbrushes it draws part of its water and minerals from the roots of neighboring plants, so it rarely thrives when grown alone in cultivated beds without a compatible grass or shrub host nearby. It is best established by interseeding into an existing dry meadow or sagebrush planting rather than transplanting bare-root divisions, and it tolerates heat, wind, and poor rocky soil far better than regular watering or fertile ground. Hummingbirds visit the tubular flowers through summer, making it a worthwhile addition to a xeric native wildflower meadow once a host grass is in place.

planting.note: Direct sow or set small divisions into lean, sharply drained, gritty soil in early spring; this true alpine rots quickly in rich or poorly drained ground and prefers the cool conditions of a scree bed or trough.

directions: Alpine mouse-ear forms a dense, low cushion of small, densely silver-haired leaves that stays attractive year-round, then disappears each spring under a flush of relatively large white, notch-petaled flowers held just above the foliage. It is a true high-mountain plant adapted to short, cool summers and sharp drainage, so it struggles in hot, humid, or poorly drained lowland gardens and is best reserved for an alpine trough, scree bed, or raised rock garden with gritty, mineral soil. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the cushion tight and prevent the center from opening up or rotting. It is more compact and better behaved than the larger, more vigorously spreading snow-in-summer (Cerastium tomentosum), making it suitable for small spaces where that species would be too aggressive.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall into moderately moist, average garden soil in full sun to partial shade; unlike the single-flowered wild meadow buttercup, this sterile double form sets no seed and spreads only modestly by clump offsets.

directions: This old cottage-garden selection of the European meadow buttercup bears fully double, tightly packed, button-like golden-yellow flowers on branching stems above deeply lobed foliage from late spring into midsummer, a long-cultivated heirloom once common in English border plantings under the folk name bachelor's buttons, long before the term was applied to cornflower. Because the flowers are sterile and set no seed, it spreads slowly as a well-behaved clump rather than naturalizing aggressively the way the single-flowered wild species can in damp meadows and lawns. Grow it in evenly moist but not waterlogged soil, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom and replenish planting stock. It pairs well with other traditional cottage perennials such as columbine and Siberian iris in a border that gets consistent moisture.

common_name: Rosenschleier Baby's Breath (Pink Fairy, Rosy Veil)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in deep, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; like other baby's breath cultivars it develops a deep taproot and resents being moved once established, so site it carefully while young.

directions: Rosenschleier, sold in English-language catalogs as Pink Fairy or Rosy Veil, is a compact baby's breath selection bearing clouds of small, semi-double flowers that open white and age to a soft dusty pink, creating a subtly shifting two-tone haze over the plant through summer. Its shorter, more mounded habit compared to taller cultivars like Bristol Fairy makes it useful toward the front or middle of a sunny border where the airy texture and pastel coloring can soften bolder neighboring flowers without needing staking. Plant in deep, lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil and avoid disturbing the taproot once established, since mature plants rarely transplant successfully. Cut stems for fresh or dried arrangements, or leave spent flower sprays in place through late summer for continued airy structure in the border.
